name: Ivan Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on the extrusion line at Hollis Aluminium, the plant out by the ring road, and I've been there fourteen months. Before that I drove city buses for sixteen years, so I'm the oldest new boy on the floor. A normal day, I'm on the saw and the stretcher at the end of the press, cutting the window profiles to length, checking them with the gauge and stacking them on the racks. I'm still learning to run the press itself, and Bogdan, our shop steward, keeps telling me to stop staring at the billet temperature like it's going to bite me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that at the end of a shift there's a rack of metal that wasn't there before. On the buses all I had to show for a day was a sore back and complaints. What wears me out is the noise and the heat by the press, and the night shifts, which pay well but turn me into a ghost at home. Marta works nights on the cardiac ward too, some weeks, so the kids, Lena and Tomas, get a lot of cereal for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, let the bosses play with their chatbots and leave the press alone. At break I'd probably make a joke that the only thing AI ever automated at Hollis was the rota, and it got that wrong. Online I don't say much, I'm not on those sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and I keep learning the press. That's what I want. I came here because I wanted something steady after the bus company cut half the night routes, and this would be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep doing what he's doing, which is getting signed off on the press before next summer. Maybe the extra pay from that goes on the mortgage. I wouldn't change anything else, why would I?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, I think. Like when the doctor says it's just a pulled muscle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rota got automated. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they brought in some app that does the shift pattern. It put me on three nights, then a morning, then two nights, and Bogdan took it to the manager with the union. They went back to the paper sheet on the canteen wall for our line. That's the kind of thing I mean: the machines mess it up, and people sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything about the job you'd still want to be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the night premium to stay where it is, because that's why we can save. And I'd want them to fix the fume extractor by the ageing oven, which has been broken since I started. That's my AI Plateau wish list: a fan and a fair rota.

S0.say: I'd joke that the only thing AI ever automated at Hollis was the rota, and it got that wrong. I'd tell people to leave the press alone and let the bosses play with their chatbots.
S0.think: It means I keep the steady job I came for after the bus company cut the night routes. I just want to carry on learning the press without anything new being thrown at me.
S0.do: Keeps working towards his sign-off on the extrusion press before next summer. Puts any extra pay from the sign-off towards the mortgage and changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Relieved, like getting good news from the doctor.
S0.quote: That's my AI Plateau wish list: a fan and a fair rota.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is a former bus driver who sees technology through one story: the shift app that the union got thrown out. In his mind, machines make mistakes and people, especially organised people, fix them. With no change coming, his wishes are small and physical, which says a lot about what he values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what Bogdan would say: if the company makes more money from robots, the workers should get a share, and nobody gets pushed out the door without a proper deal. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it in the canteen. I'd be one of the loud ones, which is not like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know who goes first, and it's me. The end of the line is cutting, gauging and stacking, and that's exactly what a robot arm does. Bogdan has twenty years on the press, so they'll keep him to babysit the machines, and they'll let the fourteen-month guy go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go to every union meeting and push for a written deal on retraining and redundancy before any robot is bolted down. He'd put another few hundred a month into savings on top of the eight months they already have. He would not take an online course, and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, because there are other plants around here, but I can see it coming down the line like a bus that's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not the online course? You'd have the time to see it coming here.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I did one when I left the buses, a forklift theory course on the computer, and I failed the quiz twice before Lena did it with me. I'm not proud of it. I learn with my hands next to somebody who knows, not from a screen that talks at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned other plants around here. Would you go to one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the packaging place on Mill Road and the car parts plant past the bridge, and they always have signs up. So yes, if Hollis let me go, I'd walk in somewhere else the next week. But I'd be starting from zero again at forty-five, and that's the bit that gets me.

S1.say: If the company makes more money from robots, the workers should get a share. Nobody gets pushed out the door without a proper deal, and I'd say that loudly at the union meeting and in the canteen.
S1.think: I know I'd go first, because cutting, gauging and stacking at the end of the line is exactly what a robot arm does. They'll keep the old hands to babysit the machines and let the fourteen-month guy go.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for a written retraining and redundancy deal before robots arrive. Adds a few hundred a month to savings on top of the eight months they hold, and refuses online courses.
S1.feel: Uneasy, though not scared, because there are other plants nearby; he sees the change coming like a late bus.
S1.quote: Off the record, I know who goes first, and it's me.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is about workers' shares; his private line is personal and blunt. He's clear-eyed that seniority will protect others and not him, yet he won't touch screen-based learning because of a failed course he's still embarrassed about. The nearby plants are his real safety net, more than any retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Somebody decides to buy the robots and somebody decides to let the people go, and those people have names and they're on the board. I'd be at the rally outside the town hall with a sign, and I'd want the government to tax the machines and pay people properly while it sorts itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I'm finished in that trade, and probably every trade I could do. If the robots can run the press and drive the buses, where does a man like me go? I'm not going to become a programmer in two years, I'm not going to become one in twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month he'd sit down with Marta and work out exactly how long the savings and the rent from his mother's flat would cover the mortgage, which he thinks is close to two years if they cut hard. He'd cancel the summer trip to the lake, join the union campaign for a machine tax, and ask about extra hours anywhere that still uses people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the floor going. I wouldn't sleep, I'd be up at four doing sums on the back of an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not much warning. What would you do in those two years, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down as much of the mortgage as I can and not spend a cent on anything new. I'd squeeze every night shift out of Hollis while they still need me. And I'd keep the flat, not sell it, because rent from a flat is something a robot can't take off you, at least I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's not their fault and it's not mine. Lena's thirteen, she'd ask me straight out if we're going to lose the house, and I'd have to look her in the eye. I think I'd say: not while your mother and I have breath, and then I'd go out to the car and sit there for a bit.

S2.say: This is a choice, not the weather, and the people making it have names and sit on the board. I'd be at the town hall rally asking the government to tax the machines and pay people properly while it sorts itself out.
S2.think: I'm finished in this trade, and probably in every trade I could do. If robots can run the press and drive the buses, there's nowhere left for a man like me, and I won't become a programmer.
S2.do: Works out with Marta how long savings and rent from his mother's flat cover the mortgage, about two years if they cut hard, and cancels the summer trip. Joins the union campaign for a machine tax, takes every night shift Hollis offers and keeps the flat rather than selling it.
S2.feel: Like the floor is going; he'd lose sleep doing sums at four in the morning.
S2.quote: I'm not going to become a programmer in two years, I'm not going to become one in twenty.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years' warning, Ivan's anger and fear arrive together. He blames named decision makers rather than the technology, and his response is collective and defensive: rallies, taxes, paying down debt. The rented flat has become a symbol for him of something solid that can't be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really: tax the machines, share the money, protect the workers. But with five years I'd say it louder and earlier, because there's time for the union to actually win something. I'd tell people at work, if you're not in the union, join now while it still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is worse in a way and better in a way. Better because I'd get most of the mortgage down by then. Worse because I'd have five years of watching it come and knowing I'm not the type who jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd overpay the mortgage every month for five years and aim to have it nearly gone by 2031. He'd sign up new members at the plant, starting with the young lads on the saws, and help Bogdan get a jobs agreement written before the first robot cell arrives. He'd still not do a course, but he'd let the company teach him on the machine if they offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control than the fast one. I'd have a plan, even if I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the company teach you on the machine. That's a bit different from before. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough that you can't just stand there with your arms folded the whole time. If they put a robot cell in and say, Ivan, you're on loading and fault reset, I'd do it, if someone shows me with their hands. What I won't do is go to night school and sit in front of a laptop. That's the line for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those five years look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quieter. No new car, no kitchen, the old sofa stays. Marta would probably push me to think about the hospital, porters or something, because they'll always need someone to push a bed. I'd laugh at her, then I'd think about it in the shower.

S3.say: Tax the machines, share the money, protect the workers, and say it early while the union can still win something. If you're not in the union, join now while it still matters.
S3.think: Five years helps because I'd get most of the mortgage down by then. It also hurts, because I'd spend those years watching it come, knowing I'm not the type who jumps.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage every month, aiming to have it nearly cleared by 2031, and signs up new union members, starting with the young workers on the saws. Helps the shop steward push for a jobs agreement before the first robot cell, and accepts hands-on training from the company but no classes.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more in control than in the two-year version, because he'd have a plan, even one he doesn't like.
S3.quote: I'd have five years of watching it come and knowing I'm not the type who jumps.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time moves Ivan from protest to organising, and he softens slightly on learning: he'd accept training at the machine but draws a hard line at screens. He's honest about his own resistance, which he sees as a fact rather than a choice. Marta's suggestion of hospital portering is the first escape route he doesn't dismiss outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Shorter weeks, a share of the profits, pensions earlier for people like me. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, and I'd vote on it, every single time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fifty-three when it lands. That's too young to stop and too old to start again. And I know I won't have moved by then, because I haven't moved in my whole life unless I was pushed. The mortgage would be paid, though, and that matters more than I like to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep working at Hollis and get fully signed off on the press, so he's worth more when the robots come. He'd pay the mortgage off early, push the union to bargain for an early pension bridge for over-fifties, and vote for whoever promises a machine tax. He'd also start, slowly, asking at the hospital about portering for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Less like the floor going, more like a long hill I know I have to walk up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you haven't moved unless you were pushed. With ten years, would you push yourself this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. Marta would laugh at that. Maybe I'd push myself one small step, like the hospital, because it's people and beds and corridors, not screens. That's as far as I'd go, and I'd probably wait until year eight to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Hollis, with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones, honestly. Kai on the saw is twenty-two and thinks he's got forever. Bogdan and me, we'd have something put away, but Kai spends his whole wage on his car. I'd be on at him every week for ten years, and he'd hate me for it.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time for the government to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Shorter weeks, a share of the profits and earlier pensions for people like me, and I'd vote on it every single time.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three when it lands, too young to stop and too old to start again, and I won't have moved by then. The mortgage would be paid, though, and that matters more than I like to admit.
S4.do: Gets fully signed off on the press at Hollis and pays the mortgage off early. Pushes the union to bargain for an early pension bridge for over-fifties, votes for a machine tax and, around year eight, starts asking about hospital portering.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but it feels like a long hill he has to walk up rather than the floor giving way.
S4.quote: That's too young to stop and too old to start again.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years removes the panic but not Ivan's sense that he won't change unless pushed. He's frank that he'd likely wait until year eight to make even a small move. His worry turns outward to younger colleagues with no savings, which fits his union instincts and his role as an older new starter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. With that one I don't get to finish anything: not the press, not the mortgage, not even the fight. What would help is the government saying, from day one, that people like me get paid while it's sorted out, and that the companies doing it pay for it. A machine tax, a bridge to the pension, something in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd be angry at. Not the robots. A robot is a saw with a better brain. I'd be angry at the people who'd rather pay a machine than pay Kai or me, and then tell us on the news that it's progress. I already changed jobs once because somebody in an office decided. I'd like it not to happen twice.

headlineQuote: A robot is a saw with a better brain.
portrait: Ivan Schmidt is 43, a former city bus driver who has worked on the aluminium extrusion line at Hollis Aluminium for fourteen months and is still learning to run the press. He has a nurse partner, Marta, two children, a mortgage, eight months of savings and rent from his late mother's flat. He's a committed union member who blames owners and boards, not machines, and he openly admits he only changes when pushed and won't learn from screens. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years, and anxious with five or ten years, using the extra time to pay off the house, organise and push for a machine tax.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with only two years he wouldn't get to finish anything, not the press sign-off, the mortgage or the fight.
whatWouldHelp: A clear promise from day one that displaced workers get paid while things are sorted out, funded by the companies through a machine tax, plus a bridge to the pension, in writing.
